The bible.

Your screenwriting shelf — craft books and your blueprint, for reference.

Screenplay
Syd Field

Syd Field’s Screenplay is the book that codified the modern three-act paradigm — structure as the organic flow of a well-told story, not a formula. The foundation most other models build on.

Act I — Setup p.1–30
Establish the protagonist, world, tone, and goal. Ends on the First Plot Point (~p.25–30) that spins the story into Act II.
Act II — Confrontation p.30–90
The pursuit against escalating obstacles. The antagonist sharpens; a Midpoint twist (~p.60) changes direction. Ends on the Second Plot Point.
Act III — Resolution p.90–120
The climax and the tie-off; the theme is fully expressed.
Key terms

Inciting Incident (~p.10–12) disrupts the status quo. Plot Points turn the story in a new direction. Pinch Points are mid-Act-II reminders of the stakes and the antagonist. Climax is the final confrontation.

Field’s method

Idea → logline → step outline → mark the plot points → fast first draft → rewrite with purpose. The first ten pages are everything.

Save the Cat!
Blake Snyder

Blake Snyder’s Save the Cat! — practical and no-fluff. Earn the audience’s empathy early (the “save the cat” moment); treat every story as a problem to solve. Famous for the 15-beat sheet, mapped to a ~110-page script.

  1. Opening Image (1) — visual tone-setter; what’s missing or broken.
  2. Theme Stated (5) — someone hints at the life lesson.
  3. Set-Up (1–10) — world, characters, flaws, stakes.
  4. Catalyst (12) — the inciting incident.
  5. Debate (12–25) — the hero hesitates.
  6. Break into Two (25) — the hero chooses the new world; Act II.
  7. B Story (30) — the emotional/thematic subplot.
  8. Fun and Games (30–55) — the promise of the premise.
  9. Midpoint (55) — false victory or defeat; stakes raised.
  10. Bad Guys Close In (55–75) — pressure builds; flaws resurface.
  11. All Is Lost (75) — the lowest point; a whiff of death.
  12. Dark Night of the Soul (75–85) — reflection; the emotional truth.
  13. Break into Three (85) — the new plan; rebirth.
  14. Finale (85–110) — the hero applies the lesson; climax.
  15. Final Image (110) — the mirror of the opening; proof of change.

Snyder also sorts stories into about ten genres by their machinery — Monster in the House, Golden Fleece, Dude with a Problem, Rites of Passage, and so on. Write the logline first, name the genre, outline the beats before the scenes.

Into the Woods
John Yorke

John Yorke’s Into the Woods argues every story is about change — a descent into chaos and a return to order — and reads it through a five-act model drawn from myth, drama, and psychology.

Act 1 — Exposition
World, protagonist, flaw; the inciting incident pushes them toward the unknown.
Act 2 — Rising action
The world turns hostile; the protagonist resists change. A first turning point shifts direction.
Act 3 — Midpoint
The crisis of identity — the “mirror moment.” Worldview is challenged; the hero turns from reactive to active.
Act 4 — Descent
Action is tested; false victory or defeat; the antagonist gains; the dark night.
Act 5 — Climax
The final choice; transformation (or failure); a new balance.

Core ideas: symmetry — every setup pays off; character is plot — what happens to the hero is the story; the midpoint is the spine; and dramatic irony (the audience knowing more than the character) builds suspense and empathy.

The Writer's Journey
Vogler · Campbell

Christopher Vogler’s The Writer’s Journey adapts Joseph Campbell’s monomyth into a screenwriter-friendly map. A pattern, not a formula — emotional milestones that mirror human growth.

1 · Ordinary World
Normal life; what’s missing.
2 · Call to Adventure
The disruption or challenge.
3 · Refusal of the Call
Fear and hesitation — the cost is named.
4 · Meeting the Mentor
Guidance, training, a gift.
5 · Crossing the First Threshold
Committing to the special world.
6 · Tests, Allies, Enemies
Learning the new rules; forming bonds.
7 · Approach to the Inmost Cave
Preparing for the central ordeal.
8 · The Ordeal
The crisis — a brush with death, literal or symbolic.
9 · Reward (Seizing the Sword)
Surviving and claiming the prize.
10 · The Road Back
Re-committing; consequences give chase.
11 · Resurrection
The final test; the change is proven.
12 · Return with the Elixir
Home, transformed, with something to share.

Archetypes — Hero, Mentor, Threshold Guardian, Herald, Shapeshifter, Shadow, Trickster — are roles, not fixed people. One character can wear several. The internal arc should mirror the external quest.

The Nutshell Technique
Jill Chamberlain

Jill Chamberlain’s The Nutshell Technique (2016): most failed scripts present a situation instead of telling a story. A story only exists when eight elements interlock around the protagonist’s central flaw — mapped on one page so you can see what’s not connecting.

1 · Set-up want
What they want in the opening scenes — and get at the Point of No Return. Usually the opposite of what they’ll want at the Crisis.
2 · Flaw
The central character flaw — Chamberlain calls this the most important element; it’s where the story lives.
3 · Point of no return
The one external event (~25%) that launches Act II; they get the set-up want…
4 · The catch
…but with a catch attached, designed to test the flaw.
5 · Crisis
The lowest point — the mirror-opposite of the set-up want.
6 · Climactic choice
The decision that turns them toward their strength.
7 · Strength
The positive quality that answers the flaw.
8 · Final step
The closing action that proves the growth is real.

Theme isn’t a ninth element — it emerges from the flaw → strength journey itself. First half: the protagonist doubles down on the flaw. Second half: they face the consequences and choose to change (or don’t).

Story
Robert McKee

Robert McKee’s Story is a masterclass in theory — principles, not rules. Two pillars: structure is meaning (the shape of events is how meaning is revealed), and a story is the writer’s moral argument.

Inciting Incident
The event that upsets the balance of the protagonist’s life and launches the central conflict.
Progressive Complications
Every scene escalates or deepens the conflict — nothing repeats, it evolves.
Crisis
The hardest decision of the character’s life: a true dilemma.
Climax
The final action taken in the face of crisis; it resolves the conflict.
Resolution
A brief, satisfying glimpse of the new status quo.
Controlling idea

Theme as one sentence of cause and effect — a value plus its cause: e.g. “Justice triumphs because the hero sacrifices personal gain for the greater good.” The climax is its proof.

More from McKee

Three levels of conflict — inner, personal, and extra-personal. True character is revealed in choice under pressure. A scene turns a value (love→hate, safety→danger). And the gap between expectation and result is where drama lives.

The Anatomy of Story
John Truby

John Truby’s The Anatomy of Story argues structure should grow out of character, not the reverse. His 22-step framework is a flexible set of guideposts for an organic, morally rich story.

The 22 steps (condensed)
  1. Self-revelation, need, and desire
  2. Ghost and story world
  3. Weakness and need
  4. Inciting event
  5. Desire (the external goal)
  6. Ally or allies
  7. Opponent (wants the same thing)
  8. Fake-ally opponent
  9. First revelation and decision
  10. Plan
  11. Opposition and complications
  12. Drive
  13. Attack by opponent
  14. Apparent defeat
  15. Second revelation and decision
  16. Audience revelation
  17. Third revelation and decision
  18. Gate, gauntlet, visit to death
  19. Battle
  20. Self-revelation
  21. Moral decision
  22. New equilibrium
Key concepts

Moral argument — the story argues how to live. Web of characters — each character is a different angle on the central moral question (the four-corner opposition: hero, main opponent, fake-ally, ally). Designing principle — the single organic idea behind the structure. Change is earned through moral struggle.

Creating Character Arcs
K.M. Weiland

K.M. Weiland’s Creating Character Arcs: story is change, and the arc is the engine. A character clings to a Lie, is forced to confront a Truth, and is transformed (or isn’t).

The Lie the character believes
A false belief that feels safe but holds them back.
The Truth
The lesson that overcomes the Lie.
The Ghost / Wound
The past trauma that planted the Lie.
The Want
The external goal — surface-level, shaped by the Lie.
The Need
The internal growth they must actually reach.
The three arcs

Positive change: overcomes the Lie, embraces the Truth. Flat: already holds the Truth and changes the world around them. Negative: clings to or sinks into the Lie — disillusionment, fall, or corruption.

Arc mapped to structure

Normal world (built on the Lie) → inciting event → First Plot Point (enters a world that challenges the Lie) → First Pinch Point → Midpoint (the Lie starts to break) → Second Pinch Point (relapse) → Third Plot Point (all is lost / dark night) → Climax (act on the Truth?) → Resolution (a changed world). Every scene either reinforces the Lie or pushes toward the Truth.

On Writing
Stephen King

Stephen King’s On Writing — part memoir, part masterclass. Not screenwriting-specific, but pure gold on craft, discipline, and mindset. Writing is a skill you sharpen by doing, honestly and daily.

Key practices
Write every day
Consistency over inspiration — King’s own target is ~2,000 words a day.
Read constantly
“If you don’t have time to read, you don’t have the tools to write.”
Door closed, then open
Draft for yourself; rewrite for the reader.
Start with situation
Put characters in trouble and watch what they do — don’t over-plot.
Tell the truth
Authenticity beats perfection; kill adverbs and the passive voice.

Editing: second draft = first draft minus ~10%. Read it cold after a break and cut what doesn’t serve the story. The muse shows up only when you’re already working.

The King Writing System
Stephen King

A distillation of King’s process into a working discipline — a fast, low-friction loop for getting a draft out and then cutting it into shape.

  1. Write every day — 1,500–2,000 words; no editing while drafting.
  2. Start at the most active moment; if stuck, start where things go wrong.
  3. First draft fast — don’t reread, don’t fix, don’t show anyone.
  4. Every scene must do one: something happens, conflict occurs, or new info is revealed.
  5. Scene check — who’s here, what they want, what blocks them, what changes.
  6. Dialogue reveals character or moves the scene; use “said” or no tag.
  7. Description minimal — a few strong details, no over-explaining.
  8. Start from a situation, not a full outline; let characters drive.
  9. After a draft, step away (ideally weeks) before revising.
  10. Rewrite: second draft = first minus ~10%.
  11. Cut adverbs, filler, and passive voice; strong verbs, direct sentences.
  12. Edit order: structure → character logic → language → pacing.
  13. Stop mid-momentum; resume there the next day.
  14. Overwhelmed? Pick one scene, write it badly, move on.
  15. Consistency over inspiration; simplicity over complexity; cutting creates quality.
Your Screenplay Sucks!
William Akers

William Akers’s Your Screenplay Sucks! — tough-love triage. Most scripts fail on fixable, lazy mistakes that make readers stop reading. The checklist is for a finished draft, not the first one.

Common script-killers
Bad openings
If the first five pages drag, you’re dead. Start in motion, with conflict or change.
Unclear protagonist
We should know fast who the story is about, what they want, and why to care.
No conflict
Every scene needs tension, opposition, or stakes.
Dialogue overload
Cut half, then cut again; use subtext — people rarely say what they mean.
Too much black on the page
Dense paragraphs kill rhythm; short action lines and white space.
Unfilmable writing
Don’t write what can’t be shown (“she feels sad inside”) — show it.
The pre-flight questions
  1. Is the theme stated early — but indirectly, never preached?
  2. Does the protagonist make the climactic choice, not get rescued?
  3. Is exposition hidden inside conflict or action?
  4. Are “on-the-nose” lines flagged for a rewrite?
  5. Does the opening image rhyme with the closing image?
  6. Does every scene earn its place — has the rest been cut?
  7. Does it work with the sound off (visual storytelling)?
  8. Are minor characters distinguishable in a line or two?
  9. Does want-vs-need conflict play at every act break?
  10. Have you read the whole thing aloud, end to end?

Akers’s favorite is the last one. Read it aloud — it catches what nothing else can.

The Screenwriter's Bible
David Trottier

David Trottier’s The Screenwriter’s Bible is a toolbox: structure, formatting, style, pitching, and selling in one reference — the go-to for getting a script professional.

1 · What a screenplay is
A visual, emotional medium; concept, logline, theme, genre; show, don’t tell.
2 · The spec script
Pro formatting — sluglines, action, dialogue, parentheticals — and what to leave out (camera angles, “we see”).
3 · Writing the screenplay
Idea → logline → outline → draft → revision; rewriting is the real writing.
4 · Marketing & pitching
Query letters, loglines, synopses, treatments; how to pitch yourself.
5 · Resources
Templates, glossaries, formatting quick-guides, TV notes.

Mantras: formatting is storytelling (clean pages keep the focus on your ideas); your logline is your hook; one page ≈ one minute of screen time; dialogue reveals character, it doesn’t just deliver info.

Writing Movies for Fun and Profit
Lennon & Garant

Lennon & Garant’s Writing Movies for Fun and Profit — half craft guide, half Hollywood survival manual, from the duo behind Night at the Museum and Reno 911!. Aimed at writing movies that sell.

Writing (Hollywood-style)

Start with a high-concept idea an exec gets in one sentence. Know the three acts cold. Keep it visual; cut voiceover and internal thought. Characters must want something. Keep scenes short (1.5–3 pages). End strong — your last ten pages should crush.

Selling & surviving

You’ll need an agent (query letters rarely work). Pitching is a performance — fast, funny, confident. You will rewrite, a lot. Never write without a deal. Studios want products, not art — deliver what sells and sneak your vision in. Be professional; be reliable.

Mantras: keep it under 110 pages (better, 105). “Hollywood is high school with money.” “There is no ‘they’ — the studio is not a person.”

Screenplay God
your 40-beat blueprint

Your own blueprint — Save the Cat’s beat logic fused with Weiland’s Lie → Truth arc, across four movements of ten beats each. Every beat tracks an external event and the internal Lie / Want / Need movement underneath it.

Act I — The Flawed Foundation
  1. Opening Image — a visual that encapsulates the Lie and tone.
  2. Everyday Life / Flaw — the status quo built around the Flaw.
  3. Hint at Ghost / Wound — a glimpse of the trauma that planted the Lie.
  4. Theme Emerges — the central moral question / Truth, spoken or implied.
  5. Inciting Incident — the disruption that destabilizes the comfort zone.
  6. Reaction to Disruption — the Flaw drives the response; denial.
  7. Stakes Rise — the cost of inaction; the Want sharpens.
  8. Call to Adventure / Counter Desire — Want vs. Need crossroads.
  9. Refusal of the Call — doubling down on the Lie.
  10. Plot Point 1 / Launch — an active choice to chase the Want.
Act II — The Lie in Action
  1. New World — new rules that quietly challenge the Lie.
  2. Early Wins / False Success — the Flaw seems to work.
  3. Opposing Flaw — a character who mirrors or contrasts the protagonist.
  4. Fun & Games / Escalation — full pursuit of the Want; the irony deepens.
  5. Subplots & Internal Conflicts — the Lie’s costs start to show.
  6. Rising Tension — the world resists the flawed strategy.
  7. Approach to Midpoint — hidden emotions surface.
  8. Midpoint Revelation / Collapse — the illusion shatters; a glimpse of Truth.
  9. False Hope / Regression — trying to fix things the old way.
  10. Midpoint Fallout — Lie-based choices cause more damage.
Act IIb — The Consequences of Denial
  1. New Plan / Desperation — a bold move still driven by the Want.
  2. Pinch Point 2 — external and moral pressure increases.
  3. Isolation / Internal Shift — alone; a fragile glimmer of growth.
  4. Subplots Collide / Symbolic Death — a loss that feels like death.
  5. Plans Collapse / Crisis Deepens — betrayal, shame, or real harm.
  6. Internal Collapse / Reckoning — the Ghost rises to the surface.
  7. Dark Night of the Soul — who are they without their defenses?
  8. Crisis Flip — the Truth breaks through; the Lie caused all of it.
  9. Decision to Change — choosing to act from the Truth.
  10. Second Plot Point — re-engaging the plot from internal clarity.
Act III — The Truth in Action
  1. New Strategy / Integrity — actions now reflect the Need.
  2. Final Approach — re-engaging the antagonist, Flaw no longer driving.
  3. Last Temptation — one final chance to regress.
  4. Climax Begins / Moral Choice — a test only the Truth can pass.
  5. The Final Confrontation — the Lie is shed, win or lose.
  6. Moment of Truth — one small, definitive gesture of the change.
  7. Victory or Defeat — the outer world reflects the inner arc.
  8. Emotional Fallout — subplots and relationships resettle.
  9. New Normal — the Truth now defines their life.
  10. Final Image — the opening mirrored, recontextualized by change.

Core directive
The thesis · read this first

Build every screenplay as a 40-scene pressure system. Each scene must have a goal, obstacle, conflict, value shift, new information, consequence, and end hook. Track character flaw, want, need, lie, truth, and transformation across the full structure.

Every scene must connect by cause and effect using therefore or but — never and then. Escalate personal, social, environmental, and mythic pressure across the acts.

The ending must feel surprising but inevitable because every flaw, lie, decision, and system created it.

The skeleton — 40 scenes across 4 acts
Structure · scene fields
The four acts — the pressure curve, in ten-scene movements

Act 1 · Setup · scenes 1–10. Establish the world, the flaw, the false conflict. End with an irreversible event.

Act 2A · Investigation · scenes 11–20. New world. Build a team. Uncover the first truth. Institutional resistance grows.

Act 2B · Pressure · scenes 21–30. Pressure tightens. Friends fracture. The system fights back. The midpoint truth becomes unavoidable.

Act 3 · Reckoning · scenes 31–40. Collapse. Confrontation. Sacrifice. Transformation. Final image.

What every scene slot tracks — the fixed fields beneath every scene

A scene is not a paragraph — it is a unit of pressure. To diagnose any scene, you should be able to name each of these:

  • Scene # — position in the 40-scene line.
  • Act / beat position — where you are in the pressure curve.
  • Scene purpose — the single reason this scene exists.
  • Location — the place, and what state it’s in (normal / disturbed / corrupted).
  • POV character — whose head we are in.
  • Scene goal — what the POV character is trying to do.
  • Obstacle — what stands in the way.
  • Conflict type — internal / interpersonal / institutional / cosmic.
  • Value shift — what changes from start to end (e.g. hope → fear, secret → exposed).
  • New information — what we learn.
  • Consequence — what is now true that wasn’t before.
  • End hook — the reversal, question, threat, or emotional shift that ejects us into the next scene.
  • Symbol / motif used — the recurring visual or object echoed here.
  • Cause → effect link — the “therefore / but” bridge to the next scene.
Act directives — scene-specific pressure
What each ten-scene movement must do
Act 1 · Setup · scenes 1–10
Purpose
  • establish world
  • establish flaw
  • establish false conflict
  • create first disruption
  • end with irreversible event
The protagonist thinks the story is about one problem — but the real story is underneath it.
Act 2A · Investigation · scenes 11–20
Purpose
  • enter new world
  • investigate
  • build team
  • uncover first truth
  • increase institutional resistance
Every discovery must answer one question, create one danger, and generate one new question.
Act 2B · Pressure · scenes 21–30
Purpose
  • pressure tightens
  • friends fracture
  • system fights back
  • antagonist plan becomes clearer
  • midpoint truth becomes unavoidable
The protagonist should stop reacting and start leading.
Act 3 · Reckoning · scenes 31–40
Purpose
  • collapse
  • confrontation
  • sacrifice
  • transformation
  • final image
The ending must feel surprising but unavoidable.
The guardrails — always-on rules
Eight rules · every scene · every draft

If you cut every rule but these, the structure still holds. Read them slowly. They are tools for diagnosis when a scene won’t come alive.

  1. Every scene must create consequence. If the world after the scene is identical to the world before it, the scene does not exist.
  2. Escalation beats repetition. If two scenes do the same job, one of them is a draft. Cut or merge.
  3. Mystery is delayed information. Mystery is not the absence of facts — it is the strategic withholding of them. The reader must always feel that an answer is being earned.
  4. Tension is unresolved conflict. Tension dies the moment a question is fully answered. Replace one tension with a bigger one before letting the previous one resolve.
  5. End with reversal, question, threat, or emotional shift. Never end on a resting beat. The next scene should feel inevitable in retrospect.
  6. Scene must contain goal, obstacle, conflict, change, consequence. If you can’t name all five, the scene is not a scene yet.
  7. New information should create new danger. Every revelation must raise the threat level — otherwise it is exposition, not story.
  8. Character action must cause the next event. The protagonist’s choices, not coincidence, drive the plot. Use therefore and but, never and then.
Character arc tracker
Per major character · the eight states

For every major character — not just the protagonist — you should be able to name eight things. The arc is the journey from start state to final form; everything else is the engine that gets them there.

  • Start state — who they are when we meet them.
  • Lie / flaw — the false belief they live by.
  • Want — what they think will fix things.
  • Need — what would actually fix things, which they cannot see yet.
  • Pressure applied — the forces working on them across the story.
  • Midpoint shift — the moment something cracks open.
  • Crisis choice — what they choose at the lowest point, when no easy answer exists.
  • Final form — who they are by the final image.
Diagnostic flags

Any scene where the protagonist meets any of these conditions deserves a second look:

  • has no decision to make
  • has no pressure on them
  • does not change in any direction
  • does not cause a consequence
The systems layer
Four pressure systems · tracked across all 40 scenes

A great story escalates on several layers at once. If only the plot is escalating, the story feels mechanical. If only the emotion is escalating, the story feels small. Track all four layers as separate curves rising across the 40 scenes.

Personal system
Emotion, guilt, revenge, friendship, identity. The internal weather of the protagonist.
Social system
Authority, conformity, public narrative, suppression. The institutions and the crowd.
Environmental system
Locations changing from normal → disturbed → corrupted. The world itself bends under the story’s weight.
Mythic system
Symbols becoming larger than themselves. A bus is a bus, then a tomb, then a verdict.
Scene diagnostic score
Eight axes · 1–5 each · rewrite or merge below 3

When a scene feels off but you can’t say why, score it. Five is the goal in every column — not because perfection is real, but because asking the question forces the rewrite.

  • Tension — how unresolved is the conflict at every moment?
  • Consequence — how irreversibly is the world changed by the end?
  • Character change — how visibly different is the POV character?
  • Plot movement — how far does the story’s engine advance?
  • Visual strength — could you draw a single image from this scene?
  • Mystery / reveal — what does it withhold and what does it confirm?
  • Cause / effect — how cleanly does it connect to the previous and next scene?
  • Theme pressure — how directly does it test the controlling idea?

Any scene scoring under 3 in two or more columns should be rewritten or merged with another scene.
